item.title: Social Security announces cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
item.description: The Social Security Administration announced new the new cost-of-living adjustment after the latest consumer inflation data was released on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027.

The COLA is determined using the consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W) data for the third quarter of the year, including the months of July, August and September. It aims to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security benefits isn't eroded by inflation.

On average, the COLA will increase Social Security retirement benefits by $75 per month.

"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," said Commissioner Frank Bisignano.

SOCIAL SECURITY CHIEF BISIGNANO SAYS PROGRAM WILL ‘BE AROUND FOR ANOTHER 90 YEARS’

The COLA will take effect for benefits paid for the month of January 2027, including Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI).

The 2027 COLA is the largest since 2023, when benefits got an 8.7% boost to account for the spike in CPI inflation that had occurred.

As inflation eased in the past three years, the COLA shrank accordingly and came in at 3.2% in 2024, 2.5% in 2025 and 2.8% in 2026.

CONSUMER INFLATION ROSE FASTER THAN EXPECTED IN SEPTEMBER, CPI REPORT SHOWS

The larger COLA for 2027 was driven in part by the rise in energy prices this year, which surged following the outbreak of the Iran war and have remained elevated due to disruptions in the oil and gasoline supply chain.

AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement that there's "a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last."

"That makes Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and everyday expenses," Minter-Jordan added.

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COSTS $5.3M AS HOMEOWNERSHIP, COLLEGE COSTS SURGE

The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) noted that the 3.6% COLA "will boost average benefits by about $900 per retiree but would provide an over $2,200 increase for the very richest beneficiaries."

"The highest earning couples who retired this year at their normal retirement age will enjoy a $3,600 combined increase – enough to push their combined benefits above $100,000 annually," CRFB wrote.

item.title: Consumer inflation rose faster than expected in September, CPI report shows
item.description: The Labor Department released the latest consumer price index data for September which showed CPI inflation rose further from the Fed's target for the month.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation accelerated in September as the pace of consumer price growth trended higher due to elevated energy prices.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said on Wednesday that the consumer price index (CPI) – a broad measure of how much everyday goods like gasoline, groceries and rent cost – increased 0.6% on a monthly basis and is up 3.7% from a year ago.

The monthly figure was in line with the estimates of economists polled by LSEG, while the annual figure came in hotter than the estimate of 3.6%. The monthly data rate picked up following a reading of 0.4% in August, while the annual figure also trended higher from 3.4% the prior month.

So-called core prices, which exclude volatile measurements of gasoline and groceries to better assess price growth trends, were up 0.3% on a monthly basis and 2.6% from a year ago. Both of those figures were hotter than the expectations of economists polled by LSEG, who predicted a monthly rise of 0.2% and an annual increase of 2.5%.

The monthly figure cooled slightly from August, when it rose 0.3%, while the annual figure rose from 2.4% in the previous report.

High inflation has created severe financial pressures in recent years for most U.S. households, which are forced to pay more for everyday necessities like food and rent. Price hikes are particularly difficult for lower-income Americans because they tend to spend more of their already-stretched paychecks on necessities and have less flexibility to save.

Energy prices rose 5.2% on a monthly basis in September and have increased 20.4% from last year. That increase follows a 2.1% monthly increase in August.

Gasoline prices increased 9.1% from the prior month in September and are up 34.2% on an annual basis, and the BLS noted the gasoline index accounted for over half of the monthly rise in the headline CPI. Electricity costs increased 0.2% on a monthly basis and are up 4.4% over the past 12 months.

WHY THE FED ISN'T READY TO DECLARE VICTORY ON INFLATION

Food prices were unchanged for the month of September and are up 2.5% compared with last year. The food at home index decreased 0.1% on a monthly basis and is up 1.8% from a year ago. The food away from home index rose 0.2% for the month and is up 3.5% from last year.

The meats, poultry and fish index declined 0.4% from the prior month in September, and is up 2.2% from a year ago. Beef and veal prices fell 1% in September and are up 3.5% from a year ago. Egg prices declined 1.3% in September and are down 20.6% from last year as supply normalizes after an avian flu outbreak.

The fruits and vegetables index increased 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and is up 3.7% from a year ago. Coffee prices rose 0.9% in September and are up 7.1% compared with last year.

Housing prices rose 0.4% month over month in September and are 3.2% higher than a year ago. Tenants' and household insurance costs increased 0.2% on a monthly basis and were up 3% from last year.

The transportation services index showed prices up 0.6% on a monthly basis and are up 2.7% from a year ago. Airline fares increased 1.2% from the prior month in September and are up 22.4% from last year.

FEDERAL RESERVE HIKES INTEREST RATES FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2023 AMID STUBBORN INFLATION

Vanguard senior economist Adam Schickling said that the "latest inflation report reinforces what we've been saying for several months: inflation is proving more persistent than many expected, particularly across services. While energy remains a factor, the more important story is that demand has stayed remarkably resilient."

"We're entering a phase where stronger productivity, moderating wage growth, and more price-sensitive consumers should help bring inflation lower, but patience will be required," Schickling added.

Tim Urbanowicz, chief investment strategist for innovator ETFs at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that "today's print puts the Fed's tactical breather priced into the market for October in question."

"With $100-plus crude adding friction to already sticky core prices, the latest data increasingly complicates the disinflation narrative and may limit the Fed's flexibility," Urbanowicz added.

The Federal Reserve will hold its next monetary policy meeting on October 27-28, and the market's expectation as far as interest rates shifted toward a rate hike.

The probability of the Fed leaving the benchmark federal funds rate at its current target range of 3.75% to 4% fell from 77.9% on Tuesday to 58.5% on Wednesday following the September CPI inflation report, the CME FedWatch tool showed.

The odds of a 25 basis point rate hike rose from 22.1% yesterday to 41.5% on Wednesday, the tool showed.

The benchmark S&P 500 Index fell 0.95% during Wednesday morning trading.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.13%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.42%.

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2B in penalties over money laundering compliance failures
item.description: The Treasury Department announced approximately $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America over failures to investigate suspicious transactions and comply with U.S. sanctions laws
item.content:encoded:
The Treasury Department announced approximately $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America over longstanding anti-money laundering failures and U.S. sanctions violations.

Regulators found the bank failed to adequately investigate trillions of dollars in potentially suspicious transactions despite knowing about significant compliance deficiencies.

The action includes the largest penalty in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the third-largest in the history of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

FinCEN assessed a $1.2 billion penalty against the nation's second-largest bank, which includes credit for a $750 million civil penalty imposed by the OCC. A separate $11.6 million settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) brings the combined penalties to approximately $1.21 billion.

BANK OF AMERICA TO HIRE 1,000 MORE APPRENTICES, INVEST $150M IN WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT

Bank of America said in a statement shared with FOX Business that the penalties will result in a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter financial results, reducing net income by approximately 17 cents per share.

A Bank of America spokesperson acknowledged the violations in a statement to Fox Business, saying the company has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combating financial crime.

The bank said it worked with regulators to resolve the penalties and has made substantial progress addressing the identified deficiencies.

The company also said it remains committed to completing the required improvements and will continue assisting federal and local law enforcement with financial crime investigations.

BANK OF AMERICA UNVEILS $250B INITIATIVE TO MODERNIZE US INFRASTRUCTURE

According to Treasury, Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions on time, including more than $1 billion in activity involving national security risks such as Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering connected to the southwest border.

As part of its settlement with FinCEN, the bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on certain foreign bank accounts and file suspicious activity reports.

The OCC found that the bank's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in large numbers of late suspicious activity reports involving billions of dollars. Many of those transactions showed indicators of potential money laundering.

Regulators also found that the bank knew for years it was failing to refer potentially suspicious transactions for investigation but did not correct the problems.

BOFA CEO BRIAN MOYNIHAN DISMISSES RECESSION FEARS DESPITE WALL STREET'S MOST HAWKISH FED FORECAST

The OCC first identified significant deficiencies in 2023 and issued a cease-and-desist order in December 2024 requiring the bank to strengthen its anti-money laundering program.

However, regulators found the bank continued to experience widespread breakdowns in its internal controls, including gaps that allowed potential trade-based money laundering transactions to go undetected.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould criticized the bank for failing to address the problems despite repeated warnings.

The separate OFAC settlement involved 475 apparent violations of U.S. sanctions programs targeting countries including Iran, Russia, Belarus, Burma and Somalia, as well as narcotics trafficking and global terrorism.

The violations included processing payments through sanctioned banks, allowing certain sanctioned individuals to conduct transactions and failing to promptly update federal sanctions watchlists.

CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO

As part of the enforcement action, Bank of America must work with an independent third party to review previously undetected suspicious transactions and undergo additional reviews of its anti-money laundering controls.

The bank also agreed to additional sanctions compliance commitments involving employee training, testing, audits and cooperation with federal regulators.

item.title: BlackRock expands skilled trades push with new financial wellness partnership for 75,000 apprentices
item.description: SaverLife and BlackRock launched a financial wellness app offering cash incentives and savings tools to over 75,000 skilled trades apprentices.
item.content:encoded:
SaverLife on Tuesday announced the launch of a customized version of its financial wellness app designed to support skilled trades workers through a partnership with BlackRock.

The app was funded by The BlackRock Foundation through its Future Builders initiative, which aims to support workforce development, and the SaverLife x BlackRock Future Builders app will provide customized tools to help thousands of skilled trades apprentices manage their debt, build credit and grow their savings.

The app is designed to meet the unique needs of apprentices working in the skilled trades and is now available to more than 75,000 workers through the electrical training ALLIANCE (etA), the national training partnership between the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) and the National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA).

The partnership will make union apprentices enrolled in BlackRock Future Builders programs eligible for cash incentives as they progress through the training program and build healthy financial habits.

MIKE ROWE SAYS CEOS ARE 'FREAKING OUT' OVER BARRIERS TO RECRUITING SKILLED TRADES WORKERS

"As technology reshapes our economy, we have an opportunity to rethink not only how we prepare people for the jobs of the future, but how we help them build lasting financial security through those careers," said SaverLife CEO Leigh Phillips.

"We're proud to partner with BlackRock Future Builders to bring personalized, technology-enabled financial guidance into the workforce development experience, supporting IBEW-NECA apprentices with timely guidance, motivation and practical tools to build savings and financial confidence from the start," Phillips added.

LARRY FINK CALLS FOR SOCIAL SECURITY REFORM, SAYS INVESTING A PORTION OF FUNDS COULD STRENGTHEN THE PROGRAM

SaverLife's platform leverages financial health expertise, behavioral science, real-time data and artificial intelligence to help working Americans through just-in-time financial support. 

The free SaverLife app currently supports over 800,000 Americans, with the majority saving more than they did before joining the platform.

BlackRock cited research from its Read on Retirement initiative, which found that a majority of skilled trades workers say they should be saving more for retirement, suggesting that there's an appetite for tools to help workers build their savings and prepare for long-term financial needs.

AMERICANS' RETIREMENT SAVINGS GROW AS MORE FAMILIES PARTICIPATE IN PLANS

"The skilled trades are opening doors to family-supporting careers and greater economic opportunity for millions of Americans," said John Kelly, global head of corporate affairs at BlackRock.

"At BlackRock, we believe that opportunity should translate into long-term financial security. By bringing innovative financial tools directly into the apprenticeship experience, we can help workers build toward financial success from their first paycheck and throughout their careers," Kelly added.

item.title: The housing market could finally become affordable again. Here's what it would take
item.description: A new analysis reveals housing costs could normalize within five years if mortgage rates fall to 6%, but some metro areas may wait a decade or more.
item.content:encoded:
Americans facing high housing costs could see some normalization of prices in the years ahead, though a new report cautions that the timeline varies widely based on market dynamics and across different metro areas.

Redfin released an analysis last week which found that housing costs could hypothetically return to "normal" in the next five years if mortgage rates fall to 6% and home price growth remains steady at about 2.1%.

"When we say housing costs could return to normal within five years, we don't mean prices are just going to fall off a cliff. We mean the gap between what homes cost and what people earn can close, mostly because incomes keep growing while price growth cools," Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, told FOX Business.

"That's not a quick fix, and it won't feel like one for buyers who are stuck waiting right now. But we anticipate the math will move in the right direction, and that matters," Fairweather added.

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COSTS $5.3M AS HOMEOWNERSHIP, COLLEGE COSTS SURGE

If mortgage rates were to stay around their current level of 7.5% and home price growth flattens, housing costs could normalize within about six years in a slightly longer timeline than in the scenario with lower rates and steady price growth.

If mortgage rates were to fall to 6% and price growth flattened, housing costs could return to normal in February 2029, while if prices were to decline 2% year over year with mortgage rates down to 6%, costs would normalize earlier in May 2028.

By contrast, if mortgage rates remain elevated between 7% and 8% and prices maintain their current annual growth rate of 2.1%, it could take 10 or more years for housing costs to return to normal levels.

AFFORDABLE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL A REALITY IN THESE MAJOR US CITIES

The report listed housing markets that could see a return to normalcy the soonest, with the fastest being San Jose, California; Austin, Texas; Oakland, California; Seattle, Washington; and Portland, Oregon.

About half of the metro areas Redfin analyzed could take at least a decade for housing costs to normalize, including many in the Northeast and Midwest, including Boston, the New York City area, Chicago and Milwaukee.

BABY BOOMERS ARE POISED TO UNLEASH MILLIONS OF HOMES – BUT THERE'S A CATCH FOR FIRST-TIME BUYERS

Additionally, markets with home price growth rates above the national average are also likely to take at least a decade to normalize.

"Buyers shouldn't try to time the market perfectly. If you find a home you can afford and plan to stay for a while, don't let the headlines scare you away from it," Fairweather said. "And if you can't afford to buy yet, the trend is on your side."

item.title: The American dream now costs $5.3M as homeownership, college costs surge
item.description: Homeownership costs surged 7.7% as the lifetime price of the American dream hit $5.32 million, far outpacing private sector wages and salaries.
item.content:encoded:
The cost of the American dream is rising at a faster pace than household earnings, driven by notable increases in the cost of homeownership, raising children and paying for college, according to a new report.

An analysis by Investopedia finds that the lifetime cost of the American dream rose 4.1% from 2025 to 2026, with the cost increasing by more than $208,000 from $5.11 million a year ago to $5.32 million this year.

That cost has risen faster than wages and salaries, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics data for private sector wages and salaries in the past 12 months through June increased 3.1%.

Investopedia's analysis of Census Bureau data found a full-time worker with a bachelor's degree earns about $3.6 million from age 25 to 64 without accounting for income taxes, while 20 years of the average Social Security benefit increases that total to about $4.1 million – about $1.2 million short of the American dream's cost.

AFFORDABLE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL A REALITY IN THESE MAJOR US CITIES

Homeownership costs rose the most in dollar terms, with the lifetime cost rising by over $91,000 from $1.184 million in 2025 to $1.275 million in 2026. That rise amounts to a 7.7% increase year over year.

That figure includes a 20% down payment on a median-priced single-family home of $420,000, with a 6.32% 30-year mortgage that brings the total cost with interest to about $837,000, as well as $3,057 a year in insurance costs, property taxes and 30 years of upkeep and utilities which adds another $438,000 to the price tag.

BABY BOOMERS ARE POISED TO UNLEASH MILLIONS OF HOMES – BUT THERE'S A CATCH FOR FIRST-TIME BUYERS

The cost of raising children and paying for college saw the fastest increase year over year, rising 8.9% from $876,092 in 2025 to $953,763, Investopedia found.

Other components of the American dream included in the analysis rose at a more modest pace – the lifetime costs of taking a yearly vacation and owning pets each rose 3.5%, to $186,999 and $40,772, respectively.

CEO REVEALS THE 'SIX-FIGURE JOBS' YOUNG AMERICANS ARE OVERLOOKING AMID LABOR SHORTAGE

Lifetime retirement costs rose 2.2% to $1,205,119 based on the estimated spending of a retired married couple over 20 years. The cost of a wedding increased by 1.6% to $38,800.

The cost of buying two new cars for the household, and covering costs for insurance, maintenance, registration and fuel rose 0.5% to $1,205,627 in lifetime costs.

Healthcare costs were the only category of the American dream analysis that saw lifetime expenses decrease compared with a year ago, albeit by just 0.2% to $413,271.

item.title: Mike Rowe says CEOs are 'freaking out' over barriers to recruiting skilled trades workers
item.description: From data centers to defense contractors, Mike Rowe says CEOs are "freaking out" over barriers to recruiting skilled trades workers nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
Intense demand for workers in the skilled trades is leading U.S. companies to ramp up training programs to expand their workforces and to poach workers from other companies to fill vitally needed positions.

Mike Rowe, CEO of the mikeroweWORKS Foundation, which helps the next generation get training in the skilled trades, told FOX Business that it's "been very surreal for me to watch the skilled trades come back into something like favor."

"I don't want to overstate it, but I can tell you that not a week goes by that I don't hear from the CEO of some consequential company or some industry leader who is straight up freaking out over the barriers to recruiting," Rowe said, adding that many large U.S. companies are establishing their own training programs to attract workers to the skilled trades.

"A lot of companies are doing things to grease the skids to accelerate the whole learning process," Rowe said. "Everybody is hiring, and nobody is quite sure how to come at it because they're all competing with each other for the same worker."

MIKE ROWE WARNS US WORKFORCE FACING 'PROBLEM OF THE DECADE'

Rowe said that a wide range of companies are seeking skilled workers, from tech companies building data centers and power plants amid the AI boom to defense contractors, home improvement firms, automakers, construction firms and more.

"The government's got a ton of skin in the game at this point, but so too does Ford and General Motors and every major Fortune 500 company. It's almost like a kind of singularity is happening around this issue — micro and macro," he said.

"To me, the most compelling stat is five-in-two: every year, when five tradesmen leave the workforce, two replace them. It's been that way for 12 years, so the math has caught up to us," Rowe added.

META LAUNCHES $115M SKILLED TRADES ACADEMY WITH GUARANTEED JOBS FOR GRADUATES IN 4 STATES

Rowe spoke with FOX Business after he visited DECKED's facility in Defiance, Ohio, where the company makes sliding drawer systems for pickup trucks. He added that the company is one of many that are hiring workers in the skilled trades.

DECKED shared an economic analysis comparing skilled trades workers, including electricians, HVAC technicians and plumbers, to bachelor's degree holders who don't have an advanced degree that found the trades offer a faster path to financial breakeven with less debt.

It found that trade trainees can break even in less than a year by starting to earn right after high school or after half a year to two years in trade school, given median entry-level wages. By contrast, a college graduate at the median starting salary who didn't work during school would break even in about three and two-thirds years.

CEO REVEALS THE 'SIX-FIGURE JOBS' YOUNG AMERICANS ARE OVERLOOKING AMID LABOR SHORTAGE

Rowe said that in talking to past recipients of scholarships from the mikeroweWORKS Foundation who've begun their careers in the skilled trades, "it's shocking how many welders who began three years ago are now in the mid-six figures."

"It's not shocking to me, but I see parents continually shocked. I see academics and the intelligentsia and reporters continually shocked when they see a 25-year-old who's prospering as a result of mastering a trade," he said, adding that he didn't want to "paint with too broad a brush" because the compensation varies based on the circumstances at play.

"It really is dependent on the individual, sometimes on the company, but certainly on geography too. But in general, there is a complete disconnect between the idea you can make six figures with a skilled trade among many, many people, and debunking that is an important part of level-setting the whole conversation," Rowe added.

GOOGLE PARTNERS WITH VETERANS GROUPS TO HELP 25,000 ENTER SKILLED TRADES CAREERS AMID WORKER SHORTAGE

"What I am hearing from the 3,600 people that we've assisted through mikeroweWORKS, that might be anecdotal, but that's way more compelling for me because these are people who got into the trades four or five years ago, and they're calling their shots right now," Rowe said. "They're deciding where they want to live. They're deciding how many hours they want to work a week or a month."

The intense demand for skilled workers has led companies to poach trade workers from rivals, which Rowe said may not necessarily be good for the country writ large – but can lead to a boost in earnings for those willing to move to pursue new opportunities.

"I was just in Plano and got a tour of a data center there. Met three electricians, all under 30, all making over $240,000 a year, all poached three times in the preceding 18 months from other projects," Rowe said.

"Again, that's not representative of all of it, but I never heard those stories 10, 12 years ago when we were just getting started with the scholarship program. I hear them now every single day," he added. "Big changes are happening right in front of us."

item.title: More than 82K rechargeable hand warmers recalled over fire risk
item.description: More than 82,000 rechargeable hand warmers combined from HotHands and Gobi Heat face a recall due to overheating that poses fire and burn hazards.
item.content:encoded:
More than 82,000 rechargeable hand warmers, including products sold at Target, The Home Depot and Amazon, have been recalled over fire and burn hazards, according to federal regulators.

The recall affects about 77,000 Kobayashi’s HotHands-branded rechargeable hand warmers sold in the U.S., along with approximately 77 sold in Canada. It also covers about 5,500 Gobi Heat-branded rechargeable hand warmers sold in the U.S. and about 47 sold in Canada.

"The lithium-ion battery and electrical components in the recalled hand warmers can overheat and ignite, posing a risk of serious injury from fire and burn hazards," the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission said in the recall notices.

No injuries have been reported in connection with either brand's hand warmers.

BABY BATH SEATS SOLD ON AMAZON RECALLED OVER DEADLY DROWNING HAZARD

Consumers should stop using the recalled products immediately and contact the respective companies for a full refund, according to the commission.

Kobayashi’s HotHands hand warmers are white and orange, while the Gobi Heat hand warmers are black and gray.

Both brands' hand warmers come in packs of two that can be magnetically joined together and include a charging cable.

Each hand warmer features a USB-C charging port for its built-in lithium-ion battery. The devices also have adjustable heat settings, LED indicator lights and a silicone lanyard.

The recalled HotHands hand warmers can be identified by model number H163650, which appears along with the batch number on the underside of the product. The white HotHands logo appears on the top of the device and on the product packaging.

The HotHands products were sold at various retailers, including Bass Pro Shops, Meijer, Target, The Home Depot and Amazon, from July 2025 to August 2026 for between $30 and $40.

ABOUT 1.5M RECHARGEABLE HAND WARMERS RECALLED AFTER 1 DEATH, HUNDREDS OF BURN INJURIES REPORTED

The recalled Gobi Heat hand warmers feature the brand name on the top of the item and on the product packaging, while model number UT3053 is located on the underside.

They were sold at GobiHeat.com from October 2024 through August 2026 for between $20 and $40.

The commission warned consumers not to dispose of the recalled hand warmers in household trash, curbside recycling bins or battery recycling boxes at retail and home improvement stores because of the risk of fire.

CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO

"Recalled lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently than other batteries, because they present a greater risk of fire. Your municipal household hazardous waste (HHW) collection center may accept this recalled lithium-ion battery or device for disposal," the commission said in its notices.

item.title: Baby bath seats sold on Amazon recalled over deadly drowning hazard
item.description: Baby bath seats sold on Amazon are under a recall because they are unstable and can tip over while in use, posing a risk of serious injury or even death from drowning.
item.content:encoded:
More than 2,000 baby bath seats are facing a recall over a hazard that federal regulators say could potentially cause injury or death to children.

About 2,140 ONTHEWEI-branded baby bath seats are affected by the recall, posing a risk of "serious injury or death due to drowning," the Consumer Product Safety Commission said in a notice last week.

"The recalled bath seats violate the mandatory standard for infant bath seats because they are unstable and can tip over while in use, posing a risk of serious injury or death due to drowning," the notice reads.

BABY SLEEP PRODUCT RECALLED AFTER FDA FINDS 3 TYPES OF ALCOHOL NOT LISTED ON LABEL

The affected items were sold on Amazon in April for between $40 and $50.

The bath seats were sold in gray, pink, blue and mist green colors. They have detachable restraint arms and suction cups on the underside.

"Model No: MY002" and "Date of manufacturer: 2026/1/10" are printed on a label located on the back of the item.

No injuries or deaths have been reported thus far in connection with the recall.

Consumers are urged to stop using the recalled bath seats immediately and contact ONTHEWEI for a full refund.

MORE THAN 265K RAM VEHICLES FACING RECALL OVER STEERING DEFECT, REGULATORS SAY

CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO

"Consumers will be asked to destroy the bath seat by writing in permanent marker 'RECALLED' on the front of the bath seat, disassembling it by removing the back rest and arm restraints and cutting the three suction cups on the seat’s underside" and sending a photo of the destroyed bath seat showing the marked product to the company, the recall notice says.

ONTHEWEI and Amazon did not immediately respond to FOX Business' requests for comment.

item.title: Americans' retirement savings grow as more families participate in plans
item.description: Federal Reserve data shows retirement account balances jumped 11% to a median $106,000 as 401(k) and IRA enrollment hit 54.9% of U.S. families.
item.content:encoded:
Americans stepped up their participation in retirement plans and saw their savings grow in recent years, a new analysis from the Federal Reserve finds.

The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances released a report on Friday detailing changes in U.S. family finances from 2022 to 2025 found that enrollment in retirement plans ticked up to 54.9% of families in 2025 – an increase of 0.6 percentage points since 2022.

The conditional median value of retirement accounts rose 11% from 2022 to 2025, reaching $106,000; while the conditional mean or average value rose 23% to $451,100 as of last year.

Retirement accounts remained the second-most commonly held type of financial asset among American households, including individual retirement accounts and certain employer-sponsored plans, such as 401(k), 403(b) and thrift savings accounts.

AMERICANS' AVERAGE 401(K) BALANCE REACHES RECORD HIGH, FIDELITY DATA SHOWS

Retirement savings balances increased for nearly all age groups from 2022 to 2025, the Fed's survey of consumer finances showed.

The 55-64 age group saw average balances rise from $588,500 in 2022 to $670,200 in 2025; while the 45-54 age group's retirement savings rose from $342,700 to $415,800 in that period.

The 35-44 cohort's average retirement savings balances increased from $154,800 to $182,400. While the under 35 age group's average savings fell from $53,800 to $48,400 from 2022 to 2025, they remained higher than the $43,800 average in 2016 and $38,300 in 2019.

BEWARE THE TICKING TIME BOMB HIDING IN YOUR 401(K)

The Federal Reserve's analysis noted that defined contribution and individual retirement account (IRA) plans were much more common than defined benefit plans, with enrollment rising from around 50% among the youngest families to about 65% for the oldest families in 2025.

It found that while families in all parts of the age distribution experienced some gains in defined contribution and IRA plans over the last decade, the biggest increase came from the youngest age group, which had participation increase from 42% in 2016 to near 50% in 2025.

Nearly all families owned at least one type of financial asset, as 98.9% of families in 2025 owned at least one transaction account, certificate of deposit, savings bond, other bond, stock, pooled investment fund, retirement account, cash value life insurance or other managed asset.

MOST 401(K) SAVERS MAY BE SHORT-CHANGING THEMSELVES, DATA SHOWS

That figure is little changed from 2022 and transaction accounts – including checking, savings, money market and call accounts, as well as prepaid debit cards – was the most commonly held category of financial asset in 2025, with an ownership rate of 98.7%.

Direct ownership of stocks declined from 2022 to 2025, falling from 21% of families to 19%. In 2022, the Fed's survey of consumer finances saw direct ownership of stocks rise six percentage points from 2019, which was the largest change between surveys on record.

The latest findings suggest that while some of the 2022 increase in direct stock ownership was temporary, the 2025 reading was still well above the 2019 rate of 15.2%. Conditional median stock holdings also rebounded from $16,400 to $30,000, which almost erased the fall in median stock holdings from 2019 to 2022.

item.title: Affordable starter homes are still a reality in these major US cities
item.description: Starter home prices surged 30.8% since 2019, with more than 21,000 fewer homes at entry-level prices as condos now make up a larger share of inventory.
item.content:encoded:
Starter homes have become increasingly scarce around the country relative to pre-pandemic inventory levels, though some metro areas around the country have a bigger supply for first-time home buyers.

A new analysis by Realtor.com found that the national share of starter homes fell from 38.1% of active inventory in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026, while starter home prices rose 30.8% in that period from about $260,000 to $340,000.

The report by Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones noted that the difference in inventory amounts to a gap of over 21,000 homes that would've been starter-priced today if that 2019 share held steady to date. Starter homes are defined in the report as being priced at about 80% of a metro's median list price. They're generally smaller and more accessible to first-time buyers or less affluent buyers.

Compared with the pre-pandemic housing market, condos have also taken on a larger role within the starter home segment relative to single-family homes.

BABY BOOMERS ARE POISED TO UNLEASH MILLIONS OF HOMES – BUT THERE'S A CATCH FOR FIRST-TIME BUYERS

In August 2019, condos comprised 18% of starter-price inventory around the country, with the rest being single-family homes. 

That figure rose to 20% by 2022 and continued to increase to 27.1% of starter homes being condos or town homes in August 2026.

The 100 largest metro areas in the country saw significant differences in terms of how the share of starter homes in their respective markets evolved from 2019 to 2026.

MORE HOMES, MORE PRICE CUTS – BUT BUYERS STILL AREN'T BITING AS MORTGAGE RATES CLIMB

While the share of starter homes has declined in the housing market nationally since 2019, some metro areas have seen gains since then.

Boise, Idaho, saw the largest gain in the share of starter homes in the metro area's housing market, with an increase of 4.7% from August 2019 to August 2026.

The second-largest gain among the top 100 metro areas was in Portland, Oregon, and Vancouver, Washington, with an increase of 4%.

Rounding out the top five largest gains in starter home share were Des Moines, Iowa, with 3.7%; San Jose, California, saw an increase of 2.9%; and Denver, Colorado, with a 2.5% gain.

BUYING A NEW HOME IS NOW CHEAPER THAN AN EXISTING ONE IN MANY MARKETS

Metros in the Sun Belt region haven't seen starter home inventory recover to pre-pandemic levels, with several leading the list of biggest declines through 2026.

The Columbia, South Carolina, metro saw its share of starter homes decline by 8.3% from 2019 to 2026, marking the largest percentage decline in the country over that period.

Winston-Salem, North Carolina, saw a decline of 7.5%, while Cape Coral and Fort Myers, Florida, fell 6.9%; and Augusta and Richmond County in Georgia and South Carolina fell 6.5%.

The only metro outside the South that ranked in the top five largest declines in starter home inventory was Fresno, Caliornia, where it declined 6% – equaling the decline in Greensboro and High Point, North Carolina.

item.title: Lyft agrees to $272 million settlement over California wage theft claims
item.description: Lyft has agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle a lawsuit brought by California officials over alleged wage theft and driver misclassification
item.content:encoded:
Lyft has agreed to pay $272.5 million to settle claims that it committed wage theft against California drivers in the six-year lawsuit the Golden State brought against the rideshare company.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the city attorneys of Los Angeles, San Diego and San Francisco sued Lyft in 2020 on allegations the company misclassified drivers as independent contractors between 2016 and 2020, meaning drivers were paid well below minimum wage and denied other workplace protections required under state law.

The majority of the money Lyft has agreed to pay, around $237 million, will be put in a third-party fund to be allocated to drivers. Drivers' eligibility and compensation will be based on the hours and total miles driven between April 2016 and December 2020.

LYFT TO LAUNCH NATIONWIDE FUEL SAVINGS PROGRAM AS DRIVERS FEEL PINCH FROM RISING GAS PRICES

"We are proud to announce this landmark win for workers, the largest misclassification settlement in California’s history," Bonta said in a statement. "Rideshare companies like Lyft have enjoyed massive growth and profits on the backs of drivers over the past decade, many of whom are from immigrant communities and communities of color. Lyft’s success would not be possible without the drivers Lyft sought to unfairly short-change. Hard-working employees deserve full compensation for their labor."

"We have not and will not stand by when companies attempt to shirk their legal responsibilities and deprive employees of their wages and benefits as required under California law," he continued. "We will continue to fight to empower workers, combat unfair and deceptive practices, and ensure all Californians can thrive from the fruits of their labor."

UBER ORDERED TO PAY $40M AFTER DRIVER LEAVES INTOXICATED WOMAN ON FREEWAY

The settlement still needs to be approved by the court.

Once the court approves the settlement and Lyft begins making payments to the settlement fund, eligible drivers will be notified through the third-party administrator about when they can send in their information for restitution.

"When companies misclassify their workers, they deny them critical protections and shift the burden onto taxpayers," Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto said in a statement. "This historic settlement sends a clear message: companies must follow the law, pay their fair share and play by the rules."

Despite Lyft agreeing to pay the settlement to bring an end to the lawsuit, the rideshare giant still maintains it did not engage in any wrongdoing.

"If approved, this settlement closes a chapter from a very different time, before Prop 22," Lyft said in a statement to FOX Business. "The vast majority of rideshare drivers in California have always wanted to be independent contractors, and voters affirmed that when they passed Prop 22 in 2020, giving drivers new benefits and protections while preserving their flexibility. And since then, Lyft has gone further than Prop 22 requires, becoming the only rideshare company with a fee cap."

GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE

"Lyft believes drivers have always been properly classified under the law, and we're glad to put this case behind us. We remain laser focused on helping create more earnings for drivers and more affordable rides for riders," the statement continued.

Between 2016 and 2020, Lyft reported a total revenue of $9.5 billion. Most Lyft drivers take home between $11 and $18 an hour after expenses, according to data compiled by ShiftTracker.

item.title: Jeff Bezos says socialism gains traction because of 'real affordability problems,' lack of real solutions
item.description: Jeff Bezos calls housing a simple supply and demand problem, pointing to Austin as proof that government intervention often backfires on affordability.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon and Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos explained in an interview on Wednesday why he thinks socialism is gaining traction among some politicians and voters, and what he thinks they're getting wrong.

Bezos spoke on the factory floor of Blue Origin's Space Coast facility with Fox News' Bret Baier in an interview that aired on "Special Report" and was asked about the factors driving some to embrace socialism.

"One, we do have real affordability problems. So people look at the cost of housing, for example, and it's very expensive. And so you can't pretend that there are no problems," Bezos said. "I don't think we should underestimate the problems, but we should also look at what the real solutions are."

Bezos said that housing is an important example because it's "a place where a lot of the government intervention that's happened has been counterproductive. Instead of working on the real solution, it's very common for, in the case of housing, certain politicians to point at landlords and say this is the fault of greedy landlords."

JEFF BEZOS PREDICTS AI WILL CREATE A LABOR SHORTAGE, NOT REPLACE HUMAN WORKERS ACROSS THE ECONOMY

"This isn't what's going on. Housing is a simple supply and demand situation. It's econ 101," he said, adding that "if you put in place government programs that subsidize demand and constrain supply, you are going to get high prices."

"If you can look at a counterexample, which is Austin, where over the last 10 years they've implemented many policies designed to make it easier to build houses, and they have housing prices going down in Austin," Bezos said.

THE HISTORY OF SOCIALISM IN THE US – AND WHY THE AMERICAN DREAM PREVAILS

He added that when voters are filling out their ballots, they should think about whether a politician is more focused on offering solutions to problems or pointing fingers to cast blame on their opponents.

"If there's a politician who's picking villains and pointing fingers, that probably means they don't have a solution. Because if that is a solution, instead of blaming somebody, they would be working on the solution," Bezos said.

IMMIGRANT WHO DEFENDED AMERICAN DREAM AGAINST SOCIALISM FIRES BACK AT CRITICS, WARNS: 'DON'T BE FOOLED'

The Amazon and Blue Origin founder added that if someone at one of his companies were to come into meetings and "instead of working on a root cause and a root fix and a real solution to the problem, all they did was point fingers and blame people, we'd exit them very quickly. Those people wouldn't be in our company for long."

Bezos was also asked about criticisms of billionaires made by political figures on the left of the ideological spectrum, and pushed back on the mentality of casting successful entrepreneurs as villains.

He said that he thinks there is an environment in which some people have been taught "this whole kind of oppressor-oppressed framework and that success is villainy. Success is not villainy."

item.title: Mortgage rates rise for seventh straight week, squeezing homebuyers
item.description: The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose this week to 7.4%, according to the latest Freddie Mac data released Thursday. That is up from last week's reading of 7.28%.
item.content:encoded:
Mortgage rates rose for the seventh straight week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday.

Freddie Mac's latest Primary Mortgage Market Survey, released Thursday, showed the average rate on the benchmark 30-year fixed mortgage rose to 7.4% from last week's reading of 7.28%.

The average rate on a 30-year loan was 6.3% a year ago.

BABY BOOMERS ARE POISED TO UNLEASH MILLIONS OF HOMES — BUT THERE'S A CATCH FOR FIRST-TIME BUYERS

"This increase comes amid continued upward pressure from the 10-year Treasury yield, which averaged 5.28% this week, 9 basis points higher than the week before," said Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner. "A wicked brew of inflation expectations, a broad bond market selloff, and rising fiscal deficits requiring new debt issuance is pushing bond yields higher, and mortgage rates are following."

The average rate on a 15-year fixed mortgage climbed to 6.73% from last week's reading of 6.6%.

Mortgage rates are affected by several factors, including the Federal Reserve and geopolitics. Though mortgage rates are not directly affected by the Fed's interest rate decisions, they closely track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year yield hovered around 5.22% as of Thursday afternoon.

Berner said the high rates "have the housing market spooked."

"Pending home sales fell year over year in both August and September even before rates crossed the 7% threshold, and sellers have been forced to cut prices at a rate not seen in four years," he said. "The increased costs of financing a home purchase have discouraged buyers already squeezed by affordability constraints, but those able to buy in cash are experiencing very favorable conditions, with prices down 1.4% year over year and for-sale inventory up 5.4% year over year."

item.title: California leads nation in Gen Z exodus as young residents flock to Texas
item.description: South Carolina led all states in net Gen Z gains while California lost over 58,000 young adults as affordability drove migration across state lines.
item.content:encoded:
A new report by LendingTree finds that almost 11 million Gen Z adults, or about one-in-four, moved across state lines in 2024, according to the latest Census Bureau data.

The data showed that an estimated 10.7 million of 44.6 million Gen Z adults, or 23.9% of that generation, moved to a different state or the District of Columbia in 2024. That figure is a far higher share than for any age group, with Millennials the closest at 14%, followed by Gen X at 7.2%, and Baby Boomers at 5.2%.

South Carolina had the largest influx of Gen Z adults, with a net gain of 22,843 in 2024, while Missouri added 14,063 to lead a group of four other states and the District of Columbia with net gains of at least 10,000 Gen Z adults.

California suffered the largest net loss of Gen Z adults with an outflow of 58,109 in 2024. That figure includes an estimated 19,287 who left California for Texas. Other states with large net losses of Gen Z adults were New Jersey with 37,556 and Illinois with 20,031.

BABY BOOMERS ARE POISED TO UNLEASH MILLIONS OF HOMES – BUT THERE'S A CATCH FOR FIRST TIME BUYERS

Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, told FOX Business that one-in-four Gen Z adults moving across state lines in 2024 "is an awful lot of people and it's by far the biggest percentage of any other generation."

"To a degree, I think that makes a lot of sense given that Gen Z may be moving away to college, may be moving away to start a new job, and is just generally more mobile and a little more able to kind of pick and choose when they move than other generations are," he added.

Schulz said that in terms of the states with the largest influx of Gen Z adults, there wasn't "one common thread because states as disparate as Texas and Washington and New York had among the biggest net gains."

"One thing that we did see was that there was a lot of movement, as you might imagine, when two fairly large states bordered each other. So, for example, North and South Carolina in the Charlotte area, or New York and New Jersey – places like that ended up making up for a lot of that state-to-state movement," Schulz said.

THE TOP CITIES IN AMERICA WHERE RENTING BEATS BUYING BY $1,000

Affordability concerns likely played some role in the decisions by Gen Z adults to move across state lines as they looked for places to stretch their budgets further, though there wasn't a clear trend.

"Generally speaking, states with the biggest net losses are among the more expensive states – California, Massachusetts, places like that. But also a place like Louisiana was kind of an exception to that rule," Schulz noted.

"I think we can safely say that affordability was driving at least part of this because it's no mystery that if you are looking for housing or looking for a job or just looking for an affordable place to live, there can be tremendous differences among the various states in this country," Schulz said.

"Being flexible provides you options, and when money is tight, when affordability is an issue, when inflation is rising – options are really, really important because it's easy to feel really powerless in a time when prices are high. But the truth is that you do have things that you can do to make a difference," he added.

THESE ARE AMERICA'S HOTTEST HOUSING MARKETS – SEE WHICH AREAS MADE THE LIST

Schulz said that for people considering relocating between states, there are "a million factors that go into it, and money is obviously a big one."

"But it is also about understanding the other factors that go into deciding where to live, a support system, family, if you're wanting to grow a family, do you have a support system in that area? And then things like taxes and job opportunities and so many things like that," he added.

For those considering a move to a different state, Schulz acknowledged that it's a big deal and that the "last thing you want to do is end up having to U-turn backwards because you made the wrong call."

He said that they need to take the time to understand a range of factors from "property taxes to employment opportunities to cultural opportunities to what the weather is like."

"So much more goes into what makes the place the right place to live than just the fact that it's more affordable, so it's really important that you take the time to really crunch the numbers and figure out what's a priority to you before you go," Schulz said.

item.title: Amazon to cut nearly 1,000 white-collar jobs across stores division and other units: report
item.description: Amazon's stores division bears the brunt of the latest cuts affecting employees in the U.S., India and the United Kingdom across divisions.

item.title: More than 265K Ram vehicles facing recall over steering defect, regulators say
item.description: More than 265,000 Ram ProMaster vans face a recall due to a defect that allows water to damage the power steering system with no warning given to drivers.
item.content:encoded:
Stellantis is recalling more than 265,000 Ram cargo vans over an issue with the vehicles' steering system, according to federal regulators.

About 265,512 Ram ProMaster vans with model years from 2022-2026 are affected by the recall, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said in its recall notice.

The recall impacts various van models, including 44,391 Ram 1500 ProMasters, 147,204 Ram 2500 ProMasters and 72,043 Ram 3500 ProMasters with model years from 2022-2026, as well as 1,874 Ram 3500 EV ProMasters with model years from 2024-2026.

FORD RECALLS MORE THAN 40,000 TRUCKS AND SUVS OVER VISIBILITY RISK

The defect can cause water to enter the vehicles' electric power steering wiring harness, potentially damaging the wiring and causing drivers to lose power steering assistance.

Drivers may receive no warning before losing power steering assistance, according to the NHTSA.

VOLKSWAGEN RECALLS 208,000 SUVS OVER BOLTS THAT COULD CAUSE STEERING LOSS

The NHTSA warned that damage to the steering system can increase the risk of a crash.

Stellantis NV, the maker of the vans, is aware of one non-injury accident linked to the problem, Stellantis spokesperson Frank Matyok said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO

To resolve the issue, dealers will inspect and replace the wiring harness and electronic power steering gear, if needed, free of charge.

Interim letters notifying owners of the safety risk are expected to be mailed out on November 17. Additional letters will be sent out once the final remedy is available.

item.title: Americans heating their homes this winter face a stark cost divide
item.description: EIA's winter outlook shows heating costs dropping for gas and propane homes, while electric and heating oil users face higher bills due to diverging fuel prices.
item.content:encoded:
American households have been facing higher energy prices this year and as colder weather approaches this winter, they may face higher heating bills for their homes depending on the type of fuel used.

The Energy Information Administration (EIA), the Energy Department's main analytical agency, released its winter fuels outlook on Tuesday, which said that the agency's "expectations this winter vary because of diverging trends in energy price among fuels and regional variation in forecast temperatures."

"We expect households using natural gas and propane as the primary heating fuel – collectively, about half of all U.S. households – will have lower energy expenditures this winter, primarily because of lower fuel costs," EIA wrote.

"We expect higher energy expenditures for households where the primary heating fuel is electricity or heating oil because of higher prices for those fuels," the agency added.

STRONG NATURAL GAS PRODUCTION, SUPPLIES COULD EASE PRESSURE ON WINTER HEATING BILLS

EIA's data showed that homes primarily heated by natural gas would see spending decrease by 9% compared with a year ago, with a range of forecast uncertainty across weather cases all showing spending decreases.

The West is projected to see a 7% increase in natural gas spending compared with last winter, while other regions are expected to see declines in the 10-15% range.

Propane-heated homes would spend 3% less under the forecast, with a range from a decrease of 10% to an increase of about 8%. Spending is expected to be flat in the South compared with last winter, while the Midwest and Northeast would see declines of 4% and 15%, respectively.

TRUMP ENERGY CHIEF SAYS TRUCKERS COULD SEE DIESEL RELIEF WITHIN DAYS AFTER EXECUTIVE ORDER

Heating oil expenditures are projected to rise 21% nationally under EIA's outlook, within an uncertainty range from about 15% to 35%.

Homes heated by electricity are expected to see spending rise 4% this winter, with the uncertainty range reflecting single-digit increases.

The West is projected to see a 9% rise from last winter, while the South and Midwest would each experience a 3% increase, and the Northeast would see a 3% drop, according to the outlook.

ENERGY CEO SAYS AMERICANS AREN'T BENEFITING FROM LOW PRICES BECAUSE OF ONE MAJOR ROADBLOCK

EIA said that while it expects national average temperatures to be similar to last year, its forecast assumes warmer temperatures in the Northeast after the region experienced a relatively cold winter last year, with much colder temperatures in the West after it experienced an unusually warm winter a year ago.

The forecast also assumes the Midwest and South will experience similar temperatures as last year.

The agency noted that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has "identified a strong El Niño pattern this winter, which could lead to large temperature variations from our forecast."

item.title: Immigrant who defended American dream against socialism fires back at critics, warns: 'Don't be fooled'
item.description: VP for economic policy at Independent Women Patrice Onwuka's immigrant family built wealth through free enterprise, and she says socialism's promise of equality always delivers equal poverty.
item.content:encoded:
As persistent inflation and squeezed household budgets leave millions of Americans feeling financially stretched, democratic socialist leaders are pitching rent controls and greater government involvement in the economy as an equalizer.

Patrice Onwuka, vice president for economic policy at Independent Women, is pushing back after her defense of capitalism and the American dream drew criticism online, warning Americans not to be swayed by what she calls the socialist "pipe dream."

On Aug. 26, Onwuka wrote an opinion piece for The Washington Post criticizing the socialist movement for challenging "the very ethos of what drew [her family] here." Her family immigrated legally from Montserrat in the Caribbean more than 40 years ago, arriving in Boston with just suitcases and living in a drug-ridden neighborhood before building wealth through ownership of a multifamily "fixer-upper" home.

Online commenters dismissed her defense of capitalism as "billionaire propaganda ... so tone-deaf"; "Everything you described happened under today's capitalist system"; "Capitalism already destroyed the American dream"; and "You're talking about 30 years ago ... it's not like this anymore, who are you kidding?"

"Those people who called my work 'billionaire propaganda,' well, I'm not a billionaire, so that's not what I'm talking about. And if they actually read beyond just the headline, which I doubt most did, then they would actually realize I started with my family's story of coming to this country with just a few suitcases of clothes and living in the ghetto in the 1980s," she told Fox News Digital.

SURGING DEM WITH D.S.A. TIES IS ‘EITHER A BONA-FIDE SOCIALIST, OR SHE’S NOT VERY SMART': G.O.P. REP

"Nothing was handed to us, and that's what my parents taught us, like so many people's families, instilled values about personal responsibility, about putting money aside, saving for what you want to build towards, self-denial, really working towards a goal and achieving it, and recognizing that opportunity does get dressed up as hard work," Onwuka said. "But, when you're willing to put the time and effort in, there is so much that you can do and so much you can achieve, frankly, that you can't achieve in other countries."

Onwuka said Americans feeling squeezed by inflation and household expenses should be wary of political promises that government intervention will deliver greater economic equality.

"Don't be fooled. They are going to sell you a pipe dream and play off emotions of how people are feeling about their financial positions," Onwuka said. "I get it, folks, when you hear the Census data come out that we had record-low poverty in 2025, record-high median incomes, which is really great news, but then you look at your own family budgets and feel like you don't have that extra cushion because of high gas prices and inflation not coming down to where it was prior to the pandemic — don't latch on to a new shiny object saying, 'Oh, I can make things better and everything will be equal.'"

"In their eyes, equal looks like everyone living like Jeff Bezos. Equal looks like everybody living like Elon Musk. But we all understand that there's certainly not enough money for the government to confiscate to make everyone a billionaire on day one," she continued.

"What equal ends up looking like is what it's looked like in other countries where this failed democratic socialist experiment has failed. Equal looks like bread lines. Equal looks like store shelves where you have maybe one or two items, not the plethora and variety that we have in our store shelves at very low cost. Equal looks like inflation in the thousands of percent rather than in the 3 to 5% range that we have right now."

Onwuka specifically called out the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) platform's support for universal rent control and tighter regulation of investment properties. In New York City, DSA-backed Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned on freezing rents for rent-stabilized tenants, and the city's Rent Guidelines Board later approved zero-percent increases for one- and two-year leases for rent-stabilized units.

"When you look historically at what has happened when rent control is implemented, well, the cost for providing that home — the mortgage payments, the maintenance fees, fixing pipes, fixing issues that come up — those costs continue to rise. The rent is capped, and so the amount that a landlord has to be able to keep that property in a very livable, comfortable space for their tenants, that money diminishes until it becomes nothing," Onwuka explained.

"And when it goes into the negative, then there is absolutely no reason for a landlord to continue to rent their property out. And so what you tend to have is you have a lot of vacant properties sitting unused. Because it's too expensive to fix them up and to keep a tenant in there since the rent that they can charge is artificially capped," she continued. "That is dangerous."

She further argued that rent controls can lead to property dilapidation, which she said could give the state a pretext to seize private property.

The Democratic Socialists of America did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

An August analysis from the libertarian Cato Institute estimated that the DSA platform would cost between $71 trillion and $212 trillion in new federal spending between 2027 and 2036, equivalent to 18% to 53% of U.S. GDP. The analysis also estimated that confiscating 100% of the total net worth of America's 400 richest individuals — $6.6 trillion — would cover only 3% to 9% of the plan's estimated 10-year cost.

"You start to see why their solutions actually do not work, but turn us into pretty much indentured servants to the federal government or the state government," Onwuka said.

"Government plays a role in terms of reducing the barriers that people have and the hurdles that people have to pursue opportunities," she added. "Whether you want to be a nurse or you want to be a firefighter, or you want to have your own small business, or you want to be a YouTube sensation — the government's role is not to tell you where to go. Government's role isn't even to make it harder for you to get into any of those occupations."

"The government should be looking for ways to ensure that the barriers are lowered so that you can compete, that you can pursue the education you want and that you go as far as you desire to go ... the Democratic Socialists of America, they don't have that to offer. They want to tell you what to do, what to become and limit your opportunities. And I don't want that for you, for me or for my children, or anyone's children."

item.title: Colleges are slashing tuition prices as students balk at soaring costs
item.description: Young Americans are questioning the value of a college degree, pushing schools like Emory & Henry University to slash tuition by half for students.
item.content:encoded:
Young Americans are reconsidering the value of a college degree given the high cost of college and the prospect of taking on student loan debt, which is prompting some colleges and universities to cut tuition costs to attract students and boost enrollment.

A report by Bloomberg noted that several colleges and universities have announced plans to lower their tuition either this year or in the next academic year when students arrive on campus in fall 2027. For example, Emory & Henry University historically offered significant merit scholarships amounting to up to $23,000 to help students negate some of the $40,000 price tag they faced, the report noted.

However, the school moved to reduce tuition by half to $19,900 for undergraduate students this academic year to lower the sticker price students are evaluating, while still offering merit scholarships up to $5,000 and covering tuition costs for certain in-state students from Virginia who meet income criteria.

"Our tuition reduction plan was just one piece of a larger strategic enrollment strategy," said Dr. Louise "Lou" Fincher, president of Emory & Henry University, told FOX Business. "Ultimately, we wanted our published tuition to better reflect the real cost of an Emory & Henry education."

COLLEGE PRESIDENT WARNS AI COULD STRENGTHEN EDUCATION – OR CREATE DANGEROUS SHORTCUTS: 'IT'S HOW WE MANAGE IT'

Emory & Henry brought in its largest incoming class of students in 190 years this August, with 492 students submitting deposits for the fall semester this year. That enrollment figure is a nearly 30% increase compared with the fall 2025 class.

Several other colleges and universities have announced plans to lower their tuition bills starting in the next academic year when students return in fall 2027, according to the Bloomberg report.

The University of Tulsa is also reducing tuition and fees from $54,000 to $25,000; while Concordia University, St. Paul is moving forward with a plan to cut tuition by $5,500 after it lowered prices by 33% in 2013.

"Affordability is among the most pressing issues for students and their families, and the sticker price of a college degree often prevents many students from considering applying. Our first Tuition Reset in 2013 created a better model, resulting in significant enrollment growth and improved outcomes. We are enacting our Tuition Reset 2.0 for 2027 to continue addressing affordability and access issues for students and families," Eric LaMott, Provost and COO for Concordia University, St. Paul, told FOX Business.

COLLEGE STUDENTS CAN NOW PAY TUITION WITH PAYPAL OR VENMO AT SOME UNIVERSITIES

Carroll College, located in Helena, Montana, consulted with Concordia on the changes it made as it evaluated how to restructure its own tuition pricing to bring in students, Bloomberg reported. Carroll ultimately chose to move forward with a plan to lower its tuition list price by 40% starting in fall 2027, while also eliminating undergraduate student fees to improve affordability.

"The new price of $26,800 makes it easier for students and families to see Carroll as a realistic option from the start," Erik Rose, associate VP of enrollment at Carroll College told FOX Business.

"Too many students ruled out Carroll before visiting campus, meeting an admission counselor or exploring financial aid because the published price appeared out of reach. We are changing that with a clearer, more transparent price so you can evaluate Carroll based on the education, opportunities, community and outcomes, not an assumption about sticker price," Rose added.

WHY 529 PLANS REMAIN A POWERFUL TOOL FOR COLLEGE, TRADE SCHOOL SAVINGS

FOX Business reached out to Tulsa University for comment.

Gerson Moreno-Riaño, president of Cornerstone University, told FOX Business that "colleges are now increasingly cutting tuition because families have little confidence in the value of a college education."

"With fewer students, more skepticism about the value of a degree, and real alternatives to a four-year campus, colleges now have to compete on price and real market value like everyone else," he added. "That's healthy."

"At Cornerstone, we saw this coming. We cut tuition 22% to $22,000 and have frozen it every year since and launched SOAR – the nation's first radically affordable, mobile-first degree and platform. Why? Because a high-quality education shouldn't require a lifetime of debt. The schools that thrive will be the ones honest about what they cost and clear about what they deliver," Moreno-Riaño said.

item.title: Workers using AI are seeing major benefits – but a gap is emerging
item.description: Artificial intelligence is helping workers complete tasks faster and more creatively, but a new job quality study finds those workplace AI benefits aren't evenly distributed.
item.content:encoded:
Workers in the U.S. who use artificial intelligence (AI) regularly in their job are seeing benefits like working more quickly or creatively, though a new study finds that those gains aren't evenly distributed across the workforce.

The American Job Quality Study, produced by Gallup, Jobs for the Future and The Families & Workers Fund from January through March, found that the majority of workers who have used AI in their job said it helps them do their jobs faster (63%), as well as to find more creative solutions to work tasks (56%).

Nearly half of respondents said it allows them to spend more time on the most interesting parts of their job (47%) or helps produce higher-quality work (46%).

However, the study also found that the benefits of using AI haven't been shared equally among workers, as workers with higher levels of educational attainment and those in managerial roles used it more than workers in other roles.

OPENAI'S SAM ALTMAN SAYS AI BENEFITS JUSTIFY ACCEPTING SOME RISKS

The American Job Quality Study found that college graduates were more than twice as likely as those without a degree to use AI on a daily or weekly basis, 40% to 17%, while 37% of managers and 25% of individual workers are regular AI users.

Molly Blankenship, associate vice president of strategy and impact at Jobs for the Future, helped lead the American Job Quality Study and told FOX Business that while workers are already reporting the benefits of using AI at work, those benefits "are not being shared evenly, they're not reaching all workers."

Blankenship noted the findings that college graduates were much more likely to use AI daily or weekly and added that those figures track with what they're seeing in terms of job quality across the U.S. workforce, as "college graduates are much more likely" to hold quality jobs than peers without degrees.

NVIDIA LAUNCHES SECURITY PLATFORM TO KEEP AI AGENTS FROM GOING ROGUE

"We find in our research that people in higher-quality jobs are more likely to be satisfied at work, are less likely to have intentions to leave, and we're seeing strong correlations between people who are using AI and who are already in quality jobs," she said.

"If we've got people who are more satisfied, more able to complete their tasks, more able to focus on the interesting parts, etc., then that's a good thing and a thing we need to promote and make as widely accessible as possible," Blankenship said. "What we're seeing in our data is that those benefits are not being shared widely, and some people aren't getting to reap the spoils of being as satisfied or engaged."

Across the workforce, the data showed that workers who used AI more frequently at work were also far more likely to report seeing it benefit their work, with 79% of regular users reporting it helped them complete tasks faster compared with 37% of irregular users.

EFFECTIVE AI GOVERNANCE DOESN'T SLOW INNOVATION, AI EXPERT TELLS HOUSE PANEL

Regular users were also more likely to report AI helping with creative solutions than irregular users (67% to 39%), producing higher-quality work (59% to 26%) and being able to focus on more interesting parts of their job (61% to 27%).

"The main benefits that people are reporting AI having for them in the workplace is the ability to do their work faster, get done and get through work faster," Blankenship said.

She added that it allows them to "produce higher-quality work even as they're moving faster, find more creative solutions to the problems that they're facing at work, and to focus on the more interesting parts of their job while letting AI support them in getting through more rote tasks."

"I think this data shows us there are a lot of people out there who are already experiencing some benefits from AI and their work. That's great. How do we make sure as we go forward that we really have an eye toward making sure that everyone gets to reap those benefits and that it can improve the work experience in America overall," Blankenship said.

item.title: Baby boomers are poised to unleash millions of homes — but there's a catch for first-time buyers
item.description: Nearly 14 million baby boomer homes will hit the housing market by 2036, but starter home supply for first-time buyers may see limited relief.
item.content:encoded:
America's housing sector is set to see nearly 14 million homes belonging to members of the baby boomer and Silent generations be released to the market over the next decade – though it may not directly lead to an influx of starter home listings, according to a new report.

An analysis by Realtor.com found that 13.9 million homes are currently owned and occupied by baby boomers and members of the Silent Generation, which are likely to be released to the housing market between 2026 and 2036.

That figure represents an increase of 33.7%, or 3.5 million homes, when compared with the prior decade's pace for older households; or an increase of 74% or 5.9 million homes over what baby boomer and Silent Generation households handed off in the last decade.

However, the influx of homes being released onto the market over the next decade will have a relatively minor impact on the supply of starter homes with two or fewer bedrooms – as a high retention rate for homes in that category means just 0.38 million are expected to be released over the next decade.

BUYING A NEW HOME IS NOW CHEAPER THAN AN EXISTING ONE IN MANY MARKETS

Realtor.com economist Jiayi Xu authored the report and told FOX Business that the "direct impact on first-time buyers of starter homes will likely be limited, because relatively few of these homes will be released onto the market."

"There is, however, a second indirect mechanism: when existing starter homeowners trade up to family-sized or large homes, their starter homes become available, which could add to starter home supply," Xu said. "Because this channel works indirectly, it will take time to materialize."

The report noted that the annualized release rate for starter homes amounts to 38,000 per year, which represents just 3.2% of starter home listings in 2026.

MORE HOMES, MORE PRICE CUTS – BUT BUYERS STILL AREN'T BITING AS MORTGAGE RATES CLIMB

The generational shift in the housing market is expected to have a larger impact on family homes, which are classified as having three or four bedrooms, with an estimated 9.9 million units released over the next 10 years. On an annual basis, the release of about 1 million family homes would account for about 24.7% of recent listings in the category.

The expected average release of 360,000 large homes per year would account for 67.2% of recent listings, and if just half reach the market (33.6%), it would mark the largest relative increase of any segment in Realtor.com's analysis and the area where the generational succession will have the most immediate impact.

The estimated 10-year retention rate among members of the boomer and Silent generations is projected at 70.7% for starter homes, compared with 61.2% for family homes and 63.6% for large homes. 

THE US CITIES WHERE HOME PRICES ARE FALLING THE FASTEST

Realtor.com noted that those dynamics are likely to contribute to weaker pricing in the family and large home segments, potentially making it more affordable for those currently living in starter homes to trade up.

"For family homes and larger homes, we expect real price softness to emerge gradually, driven by the large volume of homes these segments will release and by slower household growth on the demand side," Xu said.

"If homebuyers are looking to move up to a family home or a larger home, the timing may actually work in their favor. These two segments are expected to see a notable supply boost of all three we studied, more inventory, more negotiating power, and likely some price relief as this plays out over the next decade," Xu said.
